Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> International | National | Politics Ashantis deserve more than loans of their stolen royal regalia – Asiedu Nketiah 21 November 2026 5:33pm Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, National Chairman, National Democratic Congress (NDC), Ghana Chairman, Bureau Leadership of the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI) Member, Standing Committee of the Movement for Freedom of Nations. ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The National Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, says the Asante people deserve more than temporary access to their royal heritage, insisting that the return of looted regalia on loan from British museums cannot be equated with full restitution.
He says the distinction between a loan and a transfer of ownership is important in assessing whether communities whose cultural treasures were taken during colonial conquest have received meaningful redress.
Speaking at the Movement for Freedom of Nations Assembly in Moscow on November 16, 2026, Mr Asiedu Nketiah cited the return of Asante royal regalia for public display at the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi as an example of the complexities surrounding cultural restitution.
He acknowledged the negotiations that facilitated the arrangements but stressed that some of the objects had been fully restituted while others were only on loan from British museums.
“We appreciate the negotiations that made those arrangements possible, but a loan is not the same as a transfer of ownership,” he said.
The NDC Chairman argued that the rights restored and the obligations accepted must be central to any assessment of remedies for historical injustices.
His remarks bring renewed attention to the question of ownership of Asante royal artefacts taken during British colonial military campaigns and subsequently held in foreign museums and collections.
For the Asante people, he suggested, the return of such objects should not be judged merely by whether they can be displayed in Ghana, but also by whether ownership has been restored to the community from which they were taken.
Mr Asiedu Nketiah said claims arising from cultural seizure, enslavement, forced labour and dispossession required different forms of redress.
While the provenance and ownership of identifiable objects could be investigated, he said broader claims arising from the transatlantic slave trade raised more complex questions of responsibility, applicable law and the people entitled to benefit from reparations.
He maintained that the complexity of the issues should not be used as a reason to delay action.
“A credible claim must rest on evidence, and a credible response must be capable of implementation,” he said.
The NDC Chairman also called for communities affected by historical injustices to have a voice in the design of reparative agreements and mechanisms to hold responsible parties accountable.
He cautioned that development projects should not automatically be presented as reparations simply because they are given that description.
“The connection between the wrong and the proposed remedy must be demonstrated, and the outcome must be open to scrutiny by those asked to accept it,” he said.
Mr Asiedu Nketiah was addressing an assembly of political leaders and delegates on reparative justice and the African Union.
He urged the Movement for Freedom of Nations to support existing African Union and Caribbean reparations mechanisms rather than establish parallel institutions.
His comments come as the African Union advances its Decade of Justice and Reparations for 2026 to 2035, following its designation of 2025 as the Year of Justice for Africans and People of African Descent Through Reparations.
